extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, and writers (educated general readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical and practical evaluative principles for reading, performing, translating, and composing literature and drama (characterisation, style, dramatic proportion, logic in argument, and translation precision). Draws on 19th-century literary criticism and theatrical anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of Othello
rubrics_metrics.description: Othello must not be conceived as a negro, but a high and chivalrous Moorish chief; Shakespeare took the spirit of the character from Spanish poetry. He is majestic and composed, not ferocious; his final act is deliberate and meant to show his attachment to the Venetian state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray Othello as dignified and noble rather than as a racial caricature; emphasise internal moral struggle, honour, and composure. Avoid reducing the character to mere pigmentation or brutishness; let motive, honour, and tragic deliberation shape performance and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy as moral agony (Othello)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is not the simple point of his passion; it is an agony at discovering that one believed angelic has proved impure and worthless — a struggle not to love her; a moral indignation and regret. Iago's hints succeed because they intimate compromised honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting jealousy, frame it as an internal moral crisis and anguish over lost idealisation rather than raw animal fury. Show the preservation of love and the conflict to resist it; indicate how perceived dishonour intensifies the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity: material spectacle vs subtle incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Schiller employs a 'material sublime' — grand, external spectacles (towns on fire, infants and mothers thrown into flames) — whereas Shakespeare often achieves equal or greater effect by small, organic incidents (e.g., dropping a handkerchief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor subtle, character-driven incidents that organically produce powerful effects over gratuitous spectacle. Anti-pattern: relying on extravagant external action to manufacture sublimity rather than letting small, meaningful gestures or props carry tragic weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and proportion in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Lear is the most tremendous poetic effort, Hamlet the philosophical; Othello unites both — in Othello everything assumes its due place and proportion. By contrast, some works are gigantic but unformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for equilibrium among elements (plot, character, philosophy, passion). Mature dramatic art places each element in due proportion; avoid works that are grand in ambition but lack coherent form and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony in verse and moral-artistic consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a sad want of harmony in Lord Byron's verses; it seems unnatural to connect very great intellectual power with utter depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain formal harmony in poetry — metric, tonal, and ethical/psychological consistency between poet-persona and content. Beware dissonances between the poet's intellectual gifts and the moral tenor presented which may strain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm, non‑partisan composition yields best writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The very greatest writers write best when calm and exerting themselves on subjects unconnected with party. Political passion can reveal powers (e.g., Burke with the French Revolution) but generally partisan engagement distorts sustained literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, cultivate detachment and calm in composing literary work; reserve partisan heat for occasions when it serves a singular subject, but generally favor clarity and dispassionate craft for enduring results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of logical rigor in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: This is not a logical age; formerly premises were frequently wrong but deductions legitimate; now premises often sound but conclusions false. Preserving the study of logic (e.g., at Oxford) is commended; geometry is no substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure both sound premises and valid deductions in prose and argument. Writers should study and apply formal logical discipline to avoid sophistry or weak conclusions despite plausible premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct tragic modes among dramatists
rubrics_metrics.description: Æschylus presents religion as terrible and persecuting; Sophocles is milder though still persecuting; Euripides resembles a modern Frenchman — eager to slap at the gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and adopt the appropriate tragic temperament for a work: awe-inspiring and malignant, mild and human, or sceptical and satirical. Choose the mode that aligns with thematic aims and cultural force rather than mixing incompatible tones indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and the anti-pattern of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarists are always suspicious of being stolen from, behaving as pickpockets do with their hands in pockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for originality and avoid imitation that betrays insecurity. Anti-pattern: defensive mimicry and anxious borrowing; cultivate distinctive voice and acknowledged influences rather than covert theft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain coherent register in performance and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Kean is original but copies from himself; his rapid descents from the hyper‑tragic to the infra‑colloquial can produce effect but are often unreasonable—reading Shakespeare by flashes of lightning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid capricious, unmotivated shifts of register (from elevated to colloquial) that jar the audience. If sudden shifts are used, ensure they are artistically justified and integrated into overall dramatic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty generalities; apply principles concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir James Mackintosh is powerful in his line but deals too much in generalities and is deficient in power to apply principles to points in debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In criticism and exposition, prefer concrete application, examples, and case analysis over sweeping generalities. Demonstrate how principles operate in particulars to persuade and clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity and precision of prepositional nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators render John ch. i v.1 ('pros ton Theos') as 'with God', which is unfortunate; the preposition here implies utmost possible proximity without confusion rather than mere accompaniment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In translation choose lexical items that preserve subtle semantic and theological distinctions (proximity vs identity). Be cautious of convenience translations that flatten nuanced meaning; consult original languages and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding vs Reason — roles in composition and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The Understanding suggests the materials of reasoning; the Reason decides upon them. The former can only say 'this is or ought to be so'; the latter says 'it must be so.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or arguing, distinguish gathering/assembling evidence (understanding) from normative judgment and synthesis (reason). Structure work to reflect both processes: present materials clearly and then apply decisive, principled assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual authenticity judged by external authority and internal coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The verse of the three witnesses (1 John v.7) is likely spurious: external manuscript authority weighs against it, and its inclusion spoils the reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess textual inclusions both by external attestation and by whether they strengthen or weaken argument/logic. Anti-pattern: accept interpolations that compromise internal coherence for the sake of tradition.
